p.src: We shall leave Tang Sanzang and his disciples enduring the rainy night in a ruined building at the Huaguang Temple. Now in the county town of Diling, in Tongtai Prefecture, there was a band of villains who had squandered their property on prostitutes, drink, and gambling. With no means of supporting themselves, more than ten of them joined together as thieves and began reckoning which household in the town was the richest and which the second richest, intending to rob them of gold and silver for their expenses. One of them said, “There is no need to spy about or make elaborate plans. The household of Squire Kou, who saw those Tang monks off today, is exceedingly wealthy. Let us take advantage of this rainy night. No one in the streets will be on guard, and neither the fire wardens nor the constables will be making their rounds. We can strike at once, rob him of some capital, and then go back to whoring and gambling. Would that not be delightful?” The thieves rejoiced and agreed as one. Armed with short knives, caltrops, hooked clubs, cudgels, hempen ropes, and torches, they came through the rain, forced open the Kou family’s main gate, and charged inside with murderous shouts. Everyone in the household, old and young, male and female, fled completely out of sight in terror: the old mistress hid beneath the bed; the old master slipped behind the door; Kou Liang, Kou Dong, and their married children all scattered, trembling with fear, to save their lives. The thieves held their knives and lit their torches, broke open the household’s trunks and chests, and plundered to their hearts’ content its gold, silver, valuables, jewelry, clothing, vessels, and furnishings. Unable to bear parting with his possessions, the squire risked his life and came out, pleading with the bandits: “My lords, once you have enough for your needs, please stop. Leave this old man a few garments in which to be buried.” But the bandits would hear none of it. One rushed forward and kicked Squire Kou in the groin, knocking him to the ground. Alas! His three souls dimly departed for the realm of darkness, and his seven spirits slowly bade the mortal world farewell! Having succeeded, the thieves left the Kou residence. At the foot of the city wall they made rope ladders, fastened them one after another over the battlements, and escaped outside. Braving the rain, they fled westward through the night. Only after the thieves had withdrawn did the Kou family’s servants dare to emerge. When they looked, they saw that the old squire already lay dead upon the ground. They wailed aloud, “Heaven!” Our master has been beaten to death!” They all threw themselves over the corpse, weeping and lamenting bitterly.

p.src: That day he took his seat in court, disposed of the various official matters, and then ordered the petition board to be brought out. The Kou brothers entered clutching the board, fell to their knees, and cried, “Your Honor, we have come to report a grave case in which robbers seized property and killed a man.” The prefect received their complaint and read its allegations. Then he asked, “Yesterday I heard it said that your family had completed its vow of feeding monks and entertained four eminent holy men, arhats from the Tang court in the Eastern Land, whom you sent off through the streets with splendid music and ceremony. How then did such a thing come to pass?” Kou Liang and the others knocked their heads to the floor and said, “Your Honor, our father, Kou Hong, fed monks for twenty-four years. As these four monks had come from afar and brought the number to exactly ten thousand, he thereby completed his vow and kept them in our house for half a month. Thus they became familiar with all the roads, doors, and windows. We saw them off that day, but that very night they returned. Taking advantage of the darkness, wind, and rain, they came openly with torches and weapons, burst into the rooms, and carried off gold, silver, treasures, clothing, and jewelry. They also struck our father dead upon the ground. We beg Your Honor to obtain justice for us common people.” On hearing this, the prefect immediately mustered mounted and foot constables together with local militiamen and runners, one hundred and fifty men in all. Each bearing a sharp weapon, they left by the western gate and went straight in pursuit of Tang Sanzang and his three disciples.

p.src: Meanwhile, the master and his disciples had endured until daybreak beneath the ruined building at the Huaguang Temple. Only then did they leave and set out westward. As it happened, after robbing the Kou household that night and letting themselves down outside the city, the bandits had also taken the great western road. They traveled until dawn, passed the Huaguang Temple, and went some twenty li farther west, where they hid in a hollow among the hills to divide the gold, silver, and other spoils. Before they had finished dividing it, they suddenly saw Tang Sanzang and his three disciples approaching along the road. Their evil desires still unsated, one of the thieves pointed at Tang Sanzang and said, “Are those not the monks who were sent off yesterday?” The thieves laughed. “Excellent! Excellent! Ours is already a godforsaken trade of this sort. These monks have traveled all along the road and stayed long at the Kou residence; who knows how many valuables they carry? Let us stop them, seize their traveling money, and take their white horse to add to our shares. Would that not satisfy our every wish?” The thieves seized their weapons, raised a shout, and rushed onto the highway. Spreading out in a line, they cried, “Monks, do not move! p.src: The Pilgrim lowered his head and opened the bundle, snatched up a handful of dust from the ground, scattered it into the air, and recited a spell—the spell for fixing bodies in place. He cried, “Freeze!” The band numbered some thirty men. Every one of them stood rigidly still, teeth clenched, eyes wide, and hands spread, unable to speak or move. The Pilgrim leaped out to the road and called, “Master, come back! Come back!” Bajie panicked. “This is bad, this is bad! Elder Brother has betrayed us. He has no money on him and there is no gold or silver in the bundle, so he must be calling Master back to surrender the horse. He is calling us back to strip off our clothes too!” Sha Monk laughed. “Second Elder Brother, do not talk nonsense. Elder Brother is a man of tremendous ability. He could subdue even those vicious demons and savage monsters we met before; why would he fear these petty thieves? He must have something to tell us if he is calling from there. Let us hurry back and see.” Hearing this, the elder gladly turned the horse around. When he returned to the spot, he called, “Wukong, why did you summon us back?” The Pilgrim said, “Just look and see what these bandits have to say now.” Bajie went up, shoved one of them, and cried, “Bandit, why aren’t you moving?” The bandit was utterly insensible and said nothing. Bajie said, “Well now, he has gone deaf and dumb!” The Pilgrim laughed. “Old Sun used a body-fixing spell to hold them fast.” Bajie said, “You fixed their bodies, not their mouths. Why can’t they make a sound?” The Pilgrim said, “Master, please dismount and sit down. As the saying goes, ‘Better a mistaken arrest than a mistaken release.’ Brothers, knock all the bandits down and bind them. We will make them give a confession and find out whether they are novice robbers or practiced hands.” Sha Monk said, “But we have no rope.” The Pilgrim promptly plucked out some hairs, breathed an immortal breath over them, and transformed them into thirty ropes. They all set to work, knocked the bandits down, and bound each one hand and foot like a trussed horse. The Pilgrim then murmured the spell of release, and the bandits gradually came to their senses.

p.src: Gradually night fell. The drums sounded from the watchtower, and the fire patrol made its rounds. When the night had dragged on to the third beat of the fourth watch, Pilgrim saw that the others were no longer groaning but had all fallen asleep. He thought to himself, “My master was fated to endure this one night’s calamity in prison. That is why I neither spoke in our defense nor used my powers. Now the fourth watch is nearly over and the ordeal almost fulfilled. I must go and make the necessary arrangements so that we may leave the prison at daybreak.” Watch him display his skill: he shrank his body and slipped free of the restraint bench. With a shake of his body he changed into a grasshopper and flew out through a crack between the roof tiles beneath the eaves. The stars were bright and the moon clear; it was a mild and tranquil night. He found his bearings and flew straight toward the gate of the Kou residence. On the western side of the street he saw a house brightly lit. Flying closer to its door to look, he discovered that it was a tofu maker’s shop. He saw an old man tending the fire and an old woman pressing the soybean pulp. Suddenly the old man said, “Mother, Master Kou certainly had sons and wealth, but he had no longevity. He and I studied together as boys, though I was five years older than he. His father was named Kou Ming. In those days the family did not even own a thousand mu of land, and when he lent grain or money at interest, he could scarcely collect what was owed. When he was twenty, old Ming died, and he took charge of the family property. In truth, good fortune followed him at every step. The wife he married was the daughter of Zhang Wang, whose childhood name was Chuanzhen’er. She brought prosperity to her husband: after she entered his household, their fields yielded abundant harvests, their loans were repaid, everything they bought brought profit, and every enterprise made money. By now they had amassed a fortune of a hundred thousand. When he reached forty, he turned his heart toward goodness and provided vegetarian meals for ten thousand monks. Yet unexpectedly, last night he was kicked to death by robbers. How pitiful! He was only sixty-four this year, just at the age to enjoy his fortune. Who would have thought that despite such devotion to goodness, he would receive no good reward but die a violent death? What a lamentable thing, truly lamentable!”

p.src: Wukong listened to every word, and soon the first watch of the fifth hour sounded. He flew into the Kou residence and saw that the coffin had already been laid in the main hall. A lamp burned beside its head, with incense, candles, flowers, and fruit arranged before it, while the old lady wept nearby; he also saw the dead man's two sons come to bow and mourn, while their wives offered two bowls of rice. Wukong settled on the head of the coffin and gave a cough. The two daughters-in-law were so terrified that they flung up their hands and feet and fled outside; the brothers Kou Liang prostrated themselves on the floor, not daring to move, and merely cried, “Father! Boo-hoo-hoo...” Their mother was bolder. She struck the head of the coffin with her hand and said, “My dear husband, have you come back to life?” Imitating the old gentleman's voice, Wukong replied, “I have not come back to life.” His two sons grew more frantic still, ceaselessly kowtowing and shedding tears as they cried, “Father! Boo-hoo-hoo...” Steeling herself, their mother asked again, “Husband, if you have not come back to life, how can you speak?” Wukong said, “The King of Hell sent a ghostly messenger to escort me home so that I might speak with you. That Zhang 'Thread-the-Needle' has lied through her teeth and framed the innocent.” Hearing him call her by her childhood name, the old lady fell to her knees in alarm and kowtowed, saying, “Oh, my dear old man! At your great age, you still call me by my childhood name! What lies did I tell, and what innocent person did I harm?” Wukong shouted, “What was that tale about ‘Tang Monk setting the fire and Bajie crying murder, Friar Sand carrying off the gold and silver, and Wukong beating your father to death’? Because of your false words, good men have been made to suffer. Those four holy masters from the Tang realm met robbers on the road, recovered the stolen property, and brought it to me in gratitude. What excellent intentions they had! Yet you fabricated a complaint of theft and made your sons report them to the authorities. The authorities failed to investigate closely and have now imprisoned them. The prison god, the local earth god, and the city god were all thrown into a panic, unable to sit or stand at ease, and reported the matter to the King of Hell. The King of Hell then sent a ghostly messenger to escort me home and order you to have them released without delay; otherwise, I am to plague this household for a month and leave not one member of the family, old or young—not even a chicken or dog—alive.” The brothers Kou Liang kowtowed again and pleaded mournfully, “Father, please go back, and by all means do not harm the old or the young. At daybreak we shall go to the prefectural court and submit a petition withdrawing our accusation. We ask only that the living and the dead alike may rest in peace.” On hearing this, Wukong called out at once, “Burn some paper money. I am leaving!” The whole family came to burn paper money.

p.src: Wukong took wing again and flew straight into the prefect's residence. Looking down, he saw lamplight already shining in a room and that the prefect had risen. He flew into the central hall and saw a scroll painting hanging on the rear wall. It depicted an official riding a dappled horse, with several attendants carrying a green parasol and bearing a folding stool, though Wukong had no idea what story it represented. Wukong settled himself in the middle of it. Presently the prefect emerged from his room, bending over as he washed and combed his hair. Wukong suddenly gave a cough, frightening the prefect so badly that he fled back into his room in a panic. When he had finished washing and dressing his hair, he put on his formal robe, came out, burned incense before the painting, and prayed: “To the spirit tablet of my honored late uncle, Lord Jiang Qianyi: I, your filial nephew Jiang Kunsan, blessed by the virtue of our ancestors, was unworthily successful in the metropolitan examinations and now have the honor of serving as prefect of Tongtai Prefecture. Morning and evening I have never ceased tending your incense. Why did you utter a sound today? Pray do not become a malign spirit and frighten the household.” Wukong laughed inwardly and thought, “So this is the spirit portrait of his eldest uncle.” He promptly adopted a scriptural tone and called, “My worthy nephew Kunsan, although you owe your office to the protection of your ancestors, you have always been honest and incorruptible. Why, then, did you act so ignorantly yesterday, taking four holy monks for thieves and imprisoning them without investigating how the matter arose? The prison god, the local earth god, and the city god were disturbed and reported it to the Lord of Hell. He sent a ghostly messenger to escort me here to tell you that you must weigh the circumstances, examine the truth, and release them at once; otherwise, you will be summoned to the netherworld to answer the charge yourself.” The prefect heard this with dread in his heart and said, “Honored Uncle, please return. As soon as your nephew takes his seat in court, I shall release them.” Wukong said, “If that is so, bring paper money and burn it. I shall go report back to the Lord of Hell.” The prefect added more incense, burned paper money, and bowed in thanks.

p.src: When Wukong flew outside again and looked about, the eastern sky had already begun to pale. On reaching Diling County, he saw that all the county officials were already assembled in the hall. He thought, “If a horsefly speaks and someone sees it, the trick will be exposed. That would never do.” There in midair he transformed into a gigantic manifestation and lowered one foot from the sky until it filled the entire county court. He called out, “All you officials, listen! I am the Wandering God sent by the Jade Emperor. I am told that in your prefectural prison the Buddhist pilgrims seeking the scriptures have been tortured despite their innocence, disturbing all the gods of the Three Realms. I have been ordered to deliver this message: release them without delay! If there is the slightest delay, I shall return with another kick, first kicking to death every prefectural and county official, then trampling to death all the inhabitants of the surrounding lands, and grinding the whole city to ashes beneath my foot.” Every county official and clerk fell to his knees in panic, kowtowing and worshipping as they said, “Most holy one, please return. We shall go to the prefectural court at once, report to His Excellency the prefect, and have them released immediately. Whatever you do, do not move your foot, or you will frighten your humble officials to death.” Only then did Wukong withdraw his gigantic manifestation. He changed back into a horsefly, flew through a crack in the prison roof tiles, burrowed once more into the middle of the cangue, and went to sleep.

p.src: While he was pondering this, the magistrate of Diling County and the other officials suddenly rushed into the hall, crying in confusion, “My lord, disaster! Disaster! p.src: Before he had finished speaking, they had reached the entrance to the hall. At sight of them, the prefect, the county magistrate, and all the senior and junior officials of both administrations came down to welcome them, saying, “When the holy monks arrived yesterday, we were pressed first by the business of receiving our superior and then by the sight of the recovered loot, so we had no time to inquire closely into the truth.” Tang Monk pressed his palms together and bowed, then related the whole affair once more in detail. All the officials readily acknowledged it, saying, “We were wrong, we were wrong. Please forgive us, please forgive us.” They also asked whether anything untoward had happened in prison. The Pilgrim stepped forward, glared fiercely, and shouted in a stern voice, “Someone in this hall took my white horse, and someone in the prison took our luggage. Return them to me at once! Today it is my turn to put you to the question. What punishment do you deserve for falsely arresting innocent men as thieves?” Seeing his ferocity, every official of the prefecture and county was terrified. They immediately ordered the keeper of the horse to lead it over and the keeper of the luggage to bring it forth, returning every item to them in good order. The three disciples each displayed his fierceness, while the officials could only use the Kou family affair to excuse themselves. Let Old Sun call the dead man back to life and ask him who struck him.”

p.src: Right there in the prefectural hall, Friar Sand hoisted Tang Monk onto the horse; then, shouting and calling, they surged out together. The many prefectural and county officials also went, one and all, to the Kou residence. Kou Liang and his brothers were so terrified that they kept kowtowing before the gate as they welcomed everyone into the hall. In the mourning hall, the entire family could be seen weeping behind the funeral curtains. The Pilgrim called out, “You old woman who lied and falsely accused innocent men, stop your crying! Let Old Sun summon your husband back, ask him who killed him, and put you to shame.” The officials all thought Sun the Pilgrim was joking. The Pilgrim said, “My lords, please sit with my master for a while. Bajie and Friar Sand, guard him well. Wait here; I shall be back as soon as I have gone.” The splendid Great Sage leapt through the gate and rose straight into the sky. Rosy clouds spread over the residence on every side, while auspicious vapors filled the heavens and guarded his spirit. Only then did everyone recognize him as an immortal who rode the clouds and mist, a sage who could raise the dead and restore life. They all burned incense and bowed in worship, of which we shall say no more.

p.src: The Ten Kings of Hell came down to receive the Great Sage. After exchanging greetings, they asked why he had come and what business brought him. The Pilgrim said, “Which of you has taken the ghost of Kou Hong, the man of Diling County in Tongtai Prefecture who provided meals for monks? Look it up quickly and bring him to me.” The Ten Kings replied, “No ghostly messenger was ever sent to fetch the good man Kou Hong. He came here by himself and happened to meet Kṣitigarbha’s Golden-Robed Boy, who took him to see Kṣitigarbha.” The Pilgrim took leave of them at once and went straight to the Palace of Emerald Clouds to see Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva. After the Bodhisattva and the Pilgrim had exchanged courtesies, the Pilgrim related the whole affair. The Bodhisattva said with delight, “Kou Hong’s allotted span in the world of light had reached its fated end according to the divined number. Without taking to his sickbed, he departed this life. Because he fed monks and was a good man, I appointed him chief clerk in charge of the register of good karmic ties. Since the Great Sage has come to fetch him, I shall extend his earthly life by one cycle and have him return with you.” The Golden-Robed Boy then led Kou Hong out. When Kou Hong saw the Pilgrim, he cried again and again, “Master! Master! Please save me!” The Pilgrim said, “You were kicked to death by robbers, and this is the domain of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva in the underworld. Old Sun has come expressly to take you back to the world of the living so that the truth of this affair may be established. Since the Bodhisattva has graciously released you and extended your life by one cycle, you may return here after another twelve years.” The good squire bowed to the ground over and over without end.

p.src: The Pilgrim thanked the Bodhisattva and took his leave. He blew Kou Hong into a breath of air, tucked him into his sleeve, departed the netherworld with him, and returned to the world of light. Riding his cloud, he reached the Kou residence and immediately called on Bajie to prise open the coffin lid; then he pushed the soul back into its body. In a moment, breath issued from him and he came back to life. The squire climbed out of the coffin, kowtowed to Tang Monk and his three disciples, and said, “Masters! Masters! I, Kou Hong, died an untimely death, but through your grace I was rescued from the underworld and restored to life. You have given me life anew.” He thanked them without cease. Turning his head and seeing all the officials arrayed there, he kowtowed again and asked, “My lords, what brings all of you to my humble home?” The prefect said, “At first your son submitted a complaint about your death, naming the holy monks as the accused, so I sent men to arrest them. But it happened that the holy monks had encountered the thieves who robbed and killed your household, taken the stolen property from them, and returned it to your family. My subordinates arrested them by mistake, and before I could investigate closely, I had them sent to prison. Tonight your spirit appeared to us; my late uncle also came home to lodge an accusation; and the county received a visitation from the Wandering God descending to earth. With so many manifestations occurring at once, the holy monks were released. And now the holy monks have gone and restored you to life as well.” The squire knelt and said, “My lord, these four holy monks were indeed falsely accused. That night, more than thirty robbers came openly bearing torches and weapons and plundered my property. Unable to bear the loss, I tried to reason with them, but one of them unexpectedly kicked me in the groin and killed me. What had it to do with these four?” He summoned his wife and children and said, “Who was it that kicked me to death? How could you dare lodge a false accusation? My lord, please pronounce judgment upon them.” At this, every member of the household, old and young alike, could do nothing but kowtow. The prefect showed mercy and pardoned their offense. Kou Hong ordered a banquet prepared to thank the prefectural and county officials for their great kindness. Not one of them sat down; they all returned to their offices. The next day, Kou Hong once more hung out the sign announcing meals for monks and again urged Tripitaka to remain. But Tripitaka firmly refused to stay. So Kou Hong again invited his relatives and friends, prepared banners and canopies, and saw the pilgrims off just as before. Ah! This is precisely what is meant by:
